claim: ADHD is a common developmental disorder with a prevalence ranging from 2 to 7% in children and adolescents, averaging approximately 5%.
source: ADHD is a common developmental disorder with a prevalence ranging from 2 to 7% in children and adolescents, averaging approximately 5% (Sayal et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sayal et al., 2018.

claim: Children with ADHD often exhibit characteristics of autism spectrum disorder, such as dysfunction in social communication and social interaction.
source: In addition to the well-established core symptoms of ADHD (including the inability to sustain attention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity), some characteristics of autism spectrum disorder (ASD), such as dysfunction in social communication and social interaction, have also been frequently observed in children with ADHD (Grzadzinski et al., 2011; Mulligan et al., 2009; Reiersen et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Grzadzinski et al., 2011; Mulligan et al., 2009; Reiersen et al., 2007.

claim: Impaired theory of mind and emotion recognition are the most frequently reported social cognition deficits in children with ADHD.
source: Some studies have reported poor performance on social cognition tasks. Among these, impaired theory of mind (ToM) and emotion recognition are the most frequently reported (Bora and Pantelis, 2016; Nejati, 2022; Uekermann et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bora and Pantelis, 2016; Nejati, 2022; Uekermann et al., 2010.

claim: Social cognition in ADHD may vary depending on different factors such as general cognitive impairment, symptom severity, or age.
source: Moreover, recent studies have indicated that social cognition in ADHD may vary depending on different factors at the cognitive, pathological, or developmental levels, such as general cognitive impairment (Bora and Pantelis, 2016), symptom severity (McKay et al., 2023), or age (Bora and Pantelis, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bora and Pantelis, 2016; McKay et al., 2023.

claim: Biological motion conveys information beyond bodily movements, such as intention, emotion, sex, and identity.
source: BM, which refers to the movement of a living creature, conveys a wealth of information beyond bodily movements (Dittrich, 1993), such as intention (Pavlova, 2012), emotion (Clarke et al., 2005), sex (Kozlowski and Cutting, 1977), and identity (Jokisch et al., 2006; Loula et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Dittrich, 1993; Pavlova, 2012; Clarke et al., 2005; Kozlowski and Cutting, 1977; Jokisch et al., 2006; Loula et al., 2005.

claim: Local BM cues help identify locomotive direction and contribute to the detection of life in a visual environment.
source: Local BM cues not only help identify locomotive direction (Troje and Westhoff, 2006) but also contribute to the detection of life in a visual environment (Chang and Troje, 2008) without the observers' explicit recognition or attention (Bertenthal and Pinto, 1994; Chang and Troje, 2009a; Chang and Troje, 2009b; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Troje and Westhoff, 2006; Chang and Troje, 2008; Bertenthal and Pinto, 1994; Chang and Troje, 2009a; Chang and Troje, 2009b; Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Processing of local BM cues is less affected by attention, relatively robust to masking noise, and does not show a learning trend.
source: As a result, the processing of local BM cues is less affected by attention, relatively robust to masking noise, and does not show a learning trend (Chang and Troje, 2009a; Thornton et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang and Troje, 2009a; Thornton et al., 2002.

claim: Global BM processing involves top-down modulation, with attention playing a critical role in its perception.
source: In contrast, global BM processing involves top-down modulation, with attention playing a critical role in its perception (Thompson and Parasuraman, 2012; Thornton et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thompson and Parasuraman, 2012; Thornton et al., 2002.

claim: Global BM processing is susceptible to learning and is heavily hindered by increased mask densities.
source: Compared with local BM processing, global BM processing is susceptible to learning and is heavily hindered by increased mask densities (Thornton et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Thornton et al., 2002.

claim: Separate neural signals for local and global BM processing imply two independent BM processing stages.
source: Separate neural signals for these abilities imply two independent BM processing stages (Duarte et al., 2022; Jastorff and Orban, 2009; Vangeneugden et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Duarte et al., 2022; Jastorff and Orban, 2009; Vangeneugden et al., 2014.

claim: BM perception has received significant attention in studies on mental disorders and developmental disabilities, particularly ASD.
source: In recent years, BM perception has received significant attention in studies on mental disorders (e.g. schizophrenia Kim et al., 2013) and developmental disabilities, particularly ASD, which is characterised by deficits in social communication and social interaction (Federici et al., 2020; Todorova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Federici et al., 2020; Todorova et al., 2019.

claim: BM perception is considered a hallmark of social cognition.
source: This is because BM perception is considered a hallmark of social cognition.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Individuals with deficits in BM processing exhibit worse social perception in daily life.
source: Individuals with deficits in BM processing exhibit worse social perception in daily life (Pavlova, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pavlova, 2012.

claim: Participants' ability to process BM cues correlated with their autistic traits, particularly in the subdimension of social communication.
source: Another study found that participants' ability to process BM cues correlated with their autistic traits, particularly in the subdimension of social communication (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Children with ADHD showed reduced activity of motion-sensitive components (N200) while watching biological and scrambled motions compared with the typically developing group.
source: An EEG study found neuroelectrophysiological changes in the processing of BM stimuli in children with ADHD (Kröger et al., 2014). Specifically, compared with the typically developing (TD) group, children with ADHD showed reduced activity of motion-sensitive components (N200) while watching biological and scrambled motions, although no behavioural differences were observed.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kröger et al., 2014.

claim: Children with ADHD performed worse in BM detection with moderate noise ratios than the TD group.
source: Another study found that children with ADHD performed worse in BM detection with moderate noise ratios than the TD group (Imanipour et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Imanipour et al., 2021.

claim: Thirty-six TD children and 39 children with ADHD participated in Experiment 1.
source: Thirty-six TD children (age = 9.09 ± 2.18, 14 male) and 39 children with ADHD (age = 9.88±2.23, 28 male) participated in Experiment 1 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the study sample.

claim: The TD and ADHD groups in Experiment 1 did not differ by age but differed in sex.
source: The groups did not differ by age (t73=–1.550, p=0.126) but differed in sex (χ2=8.964, p=0.004).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical test results reported in the manuscript.

claim: Children with ADHD exhibited impaired local BM processing ability compared to TD children.
source: The results of BM-Local showed a significant difference (TD: 0.52±0.13, ADHD: 0.44±0.09, t73=3.059, p=0.003, Cohen's d=0.71), indicating that children with ADHD exhibited impaired local BM processing ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The TD group had higher accuracies than the ADHD group in BM-Global task.
source: For BM-Global and BM-General, where children were asked to detect the presence or discriminate the direction the target walker was facing, the TD group had higher accuracies than the ADHD group (BM-Global - TD: 0.70±0.12, ADHD: 0.59±0.12, t73=3.677, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.85; BM-General - TD: 0.79±0.12, ADHD: 0.63±0.17, t73=4.702, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: The TD group had higher accuracies than the ADHD group in BM-General task.
source: For BM-Global and BM-General, where children were asked to detect the presence or discriminate the direction the target walker was facing, the TD group had higher accuracies than the ADHD group (BM-Global - TD: 0.70±0.12, ADHD: 0.59±0.12, t73=3.677, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.85; BM-General - TD: 0.79±0.12, ADHD: 0.63±0.17, t73=4.702, p<0.001, Cohen's d=1.09).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 3.

claim: Children with ADHD exhibit impaired global and general BM perception.
source: These findings suggest the presence of impaired global and general BM perception in children with ADHD.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the statistical results showing lower accuracies in ADHD group.

claim: The SRS total score of the ADHD group was higher than that of the TD group.
source: The SRS total score of the ADHD group was higher than that of the TD group (SRS total score - ADHD: 54.64±18.42, TD: 38.64±12.47, t73=–4.277, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of SRS scores.

claim: Children with higher total SRS scores performed worse on the three BM tasks.
source: We found that children with higher total SRS scores performed worse on the three tasks; that is, the abilities of BM processing were negatively correlated with SRS total score (BM-Local: r=–0.264, false discovery rate [FDR]-corrected p=0.033; BM-Global: r=–0.238, FDR-corrected p=0.039; BM-General: r=–0.359, FDR-corrected p=0.006).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis of the data.

claim: The correlation between the SRS total score and the ability to process local cues was only found in the ADHD group.
source: As depicted in Figure 4, the correlation between the SRS total score and the ability to process local cues was only found in the ADHD group (ADHD: r=–0.461, FDR-corrected p=0.004; TD: r=0.109, FDR-corrected p=0.547), particularly on subscales of social awareness, social cognition, social communication, social motivation (seeTable 2 for detailed information).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4 and Table 2.

claim: No statistically significant correlation was found between the SRS total score and global or general BM processing in either the ADHD or TD groups.
source: However, we did not find a statistically significant correlation between the SRS total score and global or general BM processing in either the ADHD or TD groups (global BM perception, TD: r=–0.020, FDR-corrected p=0.910, ADHD: r=–0.207, FDR-corrected p=0.374; general BM perception, TD: r=–0.118, FDR-corrected p=0.514, ADHD: r=–0.286, FDR-corrected p=0.134).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant results.

claim: The correlation between SRS total score and response accuracy in the ADHD group was significantly stronger than in the TD group for BM-Local.
source: We observed a significantly stronger correlation between SRS total score and response accuracy in the ADHD group compared to the TD group (p=0.003) for the BM-Local, but not for the BM-Global (p=0.381) or BM-General (p=0.455).
evidence: The claim is supported by general linear model analysis comparing correlations between groups.

claim: The ability to process global BM cues was enhanced with age in the ADHD group.
source: In model (b), the ability to process global BM cues was enhanced with age (standardised β1=0.251, p=0.025).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (b).

claim: Higher FIQ, particularly on the subdimension of Perceptual Reasoning, predicted better performance in general BM processing in the ADHD group.
source: In model (c), higher FIQ, particularly on the subdimension of Perceptual Reasoning (standardised β3=0.271, p=0.005), and better performance in global BM processing (standardised β6=0.290, p=0.004) predicted better performance in general BM processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (c).

claim: Better performance in global BM processing predicted better performance in general BM processing in the ADHD group.
source: In model (c), higher FIQ, particularly on the subdimension of Perceptual Reasoning (standardised β3=0.271, p=0.005), and better performance in global BM processing (standardised β6=0.290, p=0.004) predicted better performance in general BM processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (c).

claim: As children with ADHD aged, the ability to probe general BM information improved.
source: Furthermore, as children aged, the ability to probe general BM information improved (standardised β1=0.365, p<0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (c).

claim: QbInattention showed a strong negative correlation with Perceptual Reasoning in the ADHD group.
source: It is worth noting that QbInattention showed a strong negative correlation with Perceptual Reasoning (r=–0.355, p=0.001) and general BM perception (r=–0.246, p=0.028).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: QbInattention showed a strong negative correlation with general BM perception in the ADHD group.
source: It is worth noting that QbInattention showed a strong negative correlation with Perceptual Reasoning (r=–0.355, p=0.001) and general BM perception (r=–0.246, p=0.028).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis.

claim: Sustained attention did not directly predict performance in BM-General but was significantly indirectly predicted by Perceptual Reasoning ability in the ADHD group.
source: The results indicated that sustained attention (i.e. QbInattention) did not directly predict performance in BM-General but was significantly indirectly predicted by Perceptual Reasoning ability.
evidence: The claim is supported by path analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: As children with ADHD aged, their performance in BM-General improved, both directly and through the enhanced processing of global BM cues.
source: Furthermore, as children with ADHD aged, their performance in BM-General improved, both directly and through the enhanced processing of global BM cues.
evidence: The claim is supported by path analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: In TD children, a positive relationship was observed between age and performance in BM-Global.
source: However, in models (e) and (f), we observed positive relationships between age and performance (model e: standardized β1=0.396, p=0.017; model f: standardised β1=0.330, p=0.049).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (e).

claim: In TD children, a positive relationship was observed between age and performance in BM-General.
source: However, in models (e) and (f), we observed positive relationships between age and performance (model e: standardized β1=0.396, p=0.017; model f: standardised β1=0.330, p=0.049).
evidence: The claim is supported by linear regression analysis in model (f).

claim: Children with ADHD exhibited atypical BM perception.
source: The results revealed that children with ADHD exhibited atypical BM perception.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the experimental results.

claim: Local BM processing ability was related to social interaction skills in children with ADHD.
source: Local BM processing ability was related to social interaction skills, whereas global BM processing ability significantly improved with age.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the experimental results showing correlation between local BM processing and SRS scores.

claim: Global BM processing ability significantly improved with age.
source: Local BM processing ability was related to social interaction skills, whereas global BM processing ability significantly improved with age.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the experimental results showing age-related improvement.

claim: General BM perception may be affected by sustained attentional ability in children with ADHD.
source: Critically, general BM perception (i.e. both local and global BM processing) may be affected by sustained attentional ability in children with ADHD.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the experimental results showing relationship between attention and BM perception.

claim: The relationship between sustained attention and general BM perception was primarily mediated by reasoning intelligence in children with ADHD.
source: This relationship was primarily mediated by reasoning intelligence.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the path analysis results.

claim: There is a clear association between BM perception and social cognitive abilities in TD children.
source: In TD children, there is a clear association between BM perception and social cognitive abilities (Kutsuki et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kutsuki et al., 2009.

claim: 12-month-old infants exhibit social behaviours (i.e. following gaze) elicited by BM displays.
source: For example, 12-month-old infants exhibit social behaviours (i.e. following gaze) elicited by BM displays (Yoon and Johnson, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yoon and Johnson, 2009.

claim: Sensitivity to local BM cues emerges early in life.
source: Sensitivity to local BM cues emerges early in life (Simion et al., 2008; Vallortigara et al., 2005) and involves rapid processing in the subcortical regions (Buzzell et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2018; Duarte et al., 2022; Hirai et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Simion et al., 2008; Vallortigara et al., 2005.

claim: Local BM processing involves rapid processing in the subcortical regions.
source: Sensitivity to local BM cues emerges early in life (Simion et al., 2008; Vallortigara et al., 2005) and involves rapid processing in the subcortical regions (Buzzell et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2018; Duarte et al., 2022; Hirai et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Buzzell et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2018; Duarte et al., 2022; Hirai et al., 2009.

claim: Local BM cues can guide visual attention spontaneously.
source: As a basic pre-attentive feature (Wang et al., 2010), local BM cues can guide visual attention spontaneously (Bosbach et al., 2004; Thornton and Vuong, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wang et al., 2010; Bosbach et al., 2004; Thornton and Vuong, 2004.

claim: The ability to process global BM cues is related to slow cortical BM processing and is influenced by factors such as attention and visual experience.
source: In contrast, the ability to process global BM cues is related to slow cortical BM processing and is influenced by many factors such as attention (Thompson and Parasuraman, 2012; Thornton et al., 2002) and visual experience (Chang and Troje, 2009b; Troje and Basbaum, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Thompson and Parasuraman, 2012; Thornton et al., 2002; Chang and Troje, 2009b; Troje and Basbaum, 2008.

claim: Atypical local BM processing may contribute to impaired social interactions through altered visual input.
source: Thus, atypical local BM processing may contribute to impaired social interactions through altered visual input.
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation based on the two-process theory and the study's findings.

claim: Global BM perception is enhanced with age in TD children.
source: Previous studies indicated that global BM perception is enhanced with age in TD children (Annaz et al., 2010; Ghanouni et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Annaz et al., 2010; Ghanouni et al., 2015.

claim: BM processing performance in children with ASD becomes more aligned with that of TD children as they age.
source: BM processing performance in children with ASD becomes more aligned with that of TD children as they age (Hubert et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2009; Saygin et al., 2010; Todorova et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hubert et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2009; Saygin et al., 2010; Todorova et al., 2019.

claim: The ability to process global and general BM cues improved significantly with age in both the TD and ADHD groups.
source: We found that the ability to process global and general BM cues improved significantly with age in both the TD and ADHD groups, implying that the processing module for global BM cues tends to mature with development.
evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results from models (b), (c), (e), and (f).

claim: Local BM processing is a low-level mechanism, probably performed by the primary visual cortex and subcortical regions such as the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and ventral lateral nucleus.
source: A reasonable interpretation may be that local BM processing is a low-level mechanism, probably performed by the primary visual cortex and subcortical regions such as the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and ventral lateral nucleus (Chang et al., 2018; Hirai and Senju, 2020; Loula et al., 2005), which are not malleable.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations to Chang et al., 2018; Hirai and Senju, 2020; Loula et al., 2005.

claim: The ability to process global BM cues was positively correlated with the performance in processing general BM cues in the ADHD group.
source: It is worth noting that the ability to process global BM cues was positively correlated with the performance in processing general BM cues in the ADHD group, whereas no such correlation was found in the TD group.
evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results from model (c).

claim: Children with ADHD may rely more on global BM cues to judge the direction the walker is facing when presented with both local and global BM cues.
source: This suggests that TD children are able to extract and integrate both local and global cues, whereas children with ADHD may rely more on global BM cues to judge the direction the walker is facing when presented with both local and global BM cues, which correspond to a hierarchical model (Troje and Basbaum, 2008).
evidence: The claim is an interpretation of the data supported by a citation to Troje and Basbaum, 2008.

claim: The severity of inattention in children with ADHD was negatively correlated with their performance in global BM processing.
source: Our findings are consistent with those of previous studies on the cortical processing of BM (Safford et al., 2010), as we found that the severity of inattention in children with ADHD was negatively correlated with their performance in global BM processing, whereas this significant correlation was not found in local BM processing, which may involve bottom-up processing (Hirai and Senju, 2020; Troje and Chang, 2023) and might not need participants' explicit attention (Chang and Troje, 2009a; Hirai et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by the correlation analysis and citations to Safford et al., 2010; Hirai and Senju, 2020; Troje and Chang, 2023; Chang and Troje, 2009a; Hirai et al., 2011; Thompson et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2010.

claim: Individuals with a high IQ and impaired BM perception can develop or employ reliable strategies for BM recognition, compensating for the lack of intuitive social perceptual processing.
source: One possibility is that individuals with a high IQ and impaired BM perception can develop or employ reliable strategies for BM recognition, compensating for the lack of intuitive social perceptual processing (Atkinson, 2009; Koldewyn et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Atkinson, 2009; Koldewyn et al., 2010.

claim: Children with a higher IQ, particularly in Perceptual Reasoning, demonstrated better performance in BM tasks.
source: The current study supports this assumption, as children with a higher IQ, particularly in Perceptual Reasoning, demonstrated better performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by the regression analysis results from model (c).

claim: Owing to the impact of attention deficits on Perceptual Reasoning, the performance of children with ADHD did not align with that of TD children.
source: Owing to the impact of attention deficits on Perceptual Reasoning, the performance of children with ADHD did not align with that of TD children.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation based on the correlation between attention and Perceptual Reasoning and the path analysis results.

claim: Eighty-one children met the ADHD diagnostic criteria of the DSM-5.
source: Eighty-one children met the ADHD diagnostic criteria of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the study sample.

claim: All participants in the ADHD group had a full-scale IQ >75 on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition.
source: All participants in the ADHD group had a full-scale IQ >75 (fifth upper percentile) on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition, and all TD children had a full-scale IQ above the fifth percentile on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (Pind et al., 2003), which is used to measure reasoning ability and is regarded as a non-verbal estimate of intelligence.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the inclusion criteria.

claim: All TD children had a full-scale IQ above the fifth percentile on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices.
source: All participants in the ADHD group had a full-scale IQ >75 (fifth upper percentile) on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition, and all TD children had a full-scale IQ above the fifth percentile on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (Pind et al., 2003), which is used to measure reasoning ability and is regarded as a non-verbal estimate of intelligence.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the inclusion criteria.

claim: Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices is used to measure reasoning ability and is regarded as a non-verbal estimate of intelligence.
source: All participants in the ADHD group had a full-scale IQ >75 (fifth upper percentile) on the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children-Fourth Edition, and all TD children had a full-scale IQ above the fifth percentile on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices (Pind et al., 2003), which is used to measure reasoning ability and is regarded as a non-verbal estimate of intelligence.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pind et al., 2003.

claim: Forty-two ADHD children participated in Experiment 2.
source: Forty-two ADHD children (age = 9.34±1.89, 27 male) participated in Experiment 2.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the study sample.

claim: The participants in Experiment 2 did not participate in Experiment 1.
source: The participants did not participate in Experiment 1.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the study design.

claim: The Chinese version of K-SADS-PL-C DSM-5 has demonstrated great psychometric properties.
source: The Chinese version has demonstrated great psychometric properties (Dun et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dun et al., 2022.

claim: The Chinese version of the ADHD Rating Scale has excellent psychometric properties.
source: Its Chinese version has excellent psychometric properties and consists of two subscales (Su et al., 2015): inattention (IA, nine items) and hyperactivity-impulsivity (HI, nine items).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Su et al., 2015.

claim: The psychometric properties of the Chinese version of SRS are reliable.
source: The social responsiveness scale (SRS) is a widely used quantitative measure with 65 items used to assess the severity of social impairment in many mental disorders (Constantino and Gruber, 2005), and the psychometric properties of the Chinese version are reliable (Cen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cen et al., 2017.

claim: The QB test has good measurement properties.
source: Previous psychometric studies have validated its good measurement properties (Hult et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hult et al., 2018.

claim: Point-light BM stimuli sequences adopted in this study have been used in previous studies.
source: Point-light BM stimuli sequences adopted in this study have been used in previous studies (Vanrie and Verfaillie, 2004), which were derived from the configurations of individual walking motions on a treadmill and did not contain an overall translation.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vanrie and Verfaillie, 2004.

claim: Each frame of BM sequences consisted of 13 white dots representing the human head and major joints.
source: Each frame of BM sequences consisted of 13 white dots representing the human head and major joints and was displayed on a grey background (see Video 1).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript and illustrated in Video 1.

claim: Each walking cycle lasted 1 s with 30 frames.
source: Each walking cycle lasted 1 s with 30 frames.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the stimuli.

claim: In BM-Local, scrambling disrupted the global configuration of the intact walker while retaining local kinematics.
source: Specifically, the 13 dots constituting the intact walker were randomly relocated within the original range of the BM walker (randomly presented in 2D). This manipulation disrupted the global configuration of the intact walker while retaining local kinematics.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental manipulation.

claim: In BM-Global, the two conditions (scrambled and intact walkers) contained the same local kinematics information, rendering the local motion cues uninformative.
source: Thus, the global BM component could be isolated as two conditions (i.e. scrambled and intact walkers) containing the same local kinematics information, rendering the local motion cues uninformative.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental design.

claim: In BM-Global, target walkers possibly faced one of five equally spaced directions from left to right to prevent children from learning the shape of the walker.
source: To prevent children from learning the shape of the walker (Chang and Troje, 2009a), we set target walkers that possibly faced one of five equally spaced directions from left to right.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental design, with a citation to Chang and Troje, 2009a.

claim: In BM-General, children could rely on general BM information (i.e. a combination of local and global cues) to perform the task.
source: Because the mask and target walker contained the same local BM cues and the target walker was presented with additional global configuration cues, children could rely on general BM information (i.e. a combination of local and global cues) to perform the task.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental design.

claim: The three tasks were performed in a fixed order so that the participants were naïve to the nature of the local BM cues in BM-Local.
source: We performed the three tasks in a fixed order so that the participants were naïve to the nature of the local BM cues in BM-Local.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the manuscript describing the experimental procedure.

claim: In the ADHD group, the improvement in processing general and global BM cues was greater than in processing local BM cues.
source: Interestingly, in the ADHD group, the improvement in processing general and global BM cues was greater than in processing local BM cues.
evidence: The claim is stated as a summary of the analysis comparing age-related improvements across tasks.

claim: Local BM processing is probably performed by the primary visual cortex and subcortical regions, which are not malleable.
source: A reasonable interpretation may be that local BM processing is a low-level mechanism, probably performed by the primary visual cortex and subcortical regions such as the superior colliculus, pulvinar, and ventral lateral nucleus (Chang et al., 2018; Hirai and Senju, 2020; Loula et al., 2005), which are not malleable.
evidence: The claim is an interpretation supported by citations and the observation that local BM processing does not improve with age.

claim: According to the two-process theory of biological motion processing, local BM cues guide visual attention toward BM stimuli.
source: According to the two-process theory of biological motion processing (Hirai and Senju, 2020), local BM cues guide visual attention toward BM stimuli (Bardi et al., 2011; Simion et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hirai and Senju, 2020; Bardi et al., 2011; Simion et al., 2008.

claim: Increased visual input of BM stimuli facilitates the development of the ability to process global BM cues through learning.
source: Consequently, the visual input of BM stimuli increases, facilitating the development of the ability to process global BM cues through learning (Chang and Troje, 2009a; Grossman et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang and Troje, 2009a; Grossman et al., 2004.

claim: The ability to process global BM cues is a prerequisite for attributing intentions to others and facilitating social interactions.
source: The latter is a prerequisite for attributing intentions to others and facilitating social interactions with other individuals (Chang and Troje, 2008; Frith and Frith, 1999; Troje and Chang, 2023).

claim: No impairment in BM recognition was found in individuals with autism with high IQ.
